Content covers: the two versions of the dawn-watch call (Rabbi Yishmael's 'barak barkai' versus Rabbi Akiva's 'ala barkai') and their practical difference for hiring day-laborers; Rav Safra's report of Abraham's own evening-prayer timing ('from when the walls darken') and Rashi's extended physical explanation of exactly which shadow-angle that describes; Rav Yosef's challenge to deriving halacha from Abraham's practice and its resolution via the circumcision-timing baraita (Abraham's diligence, not his legal authority, is the true derivation); Rava's own challenge reconciling the wall-darkening timing with the mishnah's fixed six-and-a-half-hour Paschal-offering schedule, resolved via the walls' imprecise verticality and either Abraham's own uniquely precise astronomical expertise (with the extended Bava Batra 16b citation on his blessing) or his standing status as an elder presiding in session; the extended baraita on elders-in-session throughout the patriarchal and Mosaic narratives; the Eliezer/Damascus notarikon and Rav's claim that Abraham fulfilled the entire Torah including rabbinic enactments not yet given (the seven Noahide laws, circumcision, and eruv tavshilin); the mishnah's ambiguity over which of the two dawn-watchers (on the roof or on the ground) actually says 'yes,' resolved via both readings and the Jerusalem Talmud's own explanation for why Hebron specifically is invoked (the merit of the patriarchs); and the extended physical explanation of why sunlight and moonlight columns are never confused, the 'cloudy day is entirely sun' teaching and its practical applications (hide-drying, Passover kneading prohibitions), and Rav Nachman's parable-pair (the sealed vinegar-jar and the leak) explaining why diffuse, filtered heat and light are harsher than their direct counterparts, closing into the start of a new teaching about impure thoughts continuing onto 29a.
